name: Puritanical bias
statement: People treat an undesirable outcome as evidence of moral weakness in the person it happened to, and judge harmless pleasure-seeking as wrong in itself.
meaning: Two definitions travel under this name and neither has a study behind it. Wikipedia's article, created on 3 April 2020, defines puritanical bias as attributing an undesirable outcome or wrongdoing to a moral deficiency or a lack of self-control rather than to broader societal determinants. A behavioural-science glossary defines it instead as over-estimating the immorality of pleasure-seeking and under-estimating the moral value of hardship, and cites nothing. The first definition is the fundamental attribution error narrowed to moralised behaviour, and that error has its own entry here. The second names something moral psychology does study, under the label puritanical morality rather than puritanical bias. A Crossref bibliographic search for the exact phrase returns a dictionary entry, literary criticism and Dutch sexual history. PubMed returns nothing. PubMed Central returns two letters to the British Medical Journal, from 1921 and 1922, on venereal disease prophylaxis. Puritanical bias is a heading rather than a finding, in the way the affinity-bias and precision-bias entries here are.

origin.where: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
origin.note: No publication coining the phrase was located. Wikipedia's opening definition rests on this commentary, which replies to Duckworth, Milkman and Laibson's review of self-control strategies in the same issue, and on a Harvard Business Review post by Michail Kokkoris and Olga Stavrova dated 16 January 2020. The commentary is behind a SAGE paywall and was not read here, so whether Loewenstein uses the phrase could not be checked. Fitouchi, Andre and Baumard's 2023 target article, which the pleasure-condemning sense of the name draws on, does not carry the phrase in its title or abstract.

evidence:
The nearest measured claim on the pleasure side is Fitouchi and Nettle's, and it is a claim about what people believe rather than about an error they make. Five pre-registered experiments with more than 3,000 American participants recruited on Prolific tested whether harmless indulgence is condemned because it is thought to erode self-control. Study 1 gave 379 participants, after 22 attention-check exclusions, a target who had increased or decreased his consumption of sex, food, alcohol and inactivity over three months without harming anyone. Indulgence was rated as lowering the target's self-control, t(193) = -28.31, and his cooperativeness, t(193) = -13.07, both p < .001, and restraint was rated as raising both. Perceived change in self-control carried the whole of the effect on perceived cooperativeness, b = 2.04, 95% CI 1.76 to 2.31, leaving a direct effect of -0.25 that was not significant. Studies 2a and 2b repeated the design with 720 and 1,200 participants split across separate domains of pleasure. Study 3 gave 500 participants a village whose council either relaxed or tightened rules on sex, food and alcohol; relaxation was expected to lower self-control and cooperation, and the prohibition was judged worse still. Study 4 described to 184 participants a study in which one group was made to increase its alcohol and pornography use. They expected that group to become less cooperative, mean -1.10 on a scale running from -3 to 3, t(183) = -13.98, p < .001, and less self-controlled, mean -1.49, t(183) = -18.33, p < .001.

The attribution side of the name has no comparable body of work under any label. What exists nearby is Uhlmann, Poehlman, Tannenbaum and Bargh's account of implicit Puritanism, which holds that Americans in particular carry Puritan-Protestant intuitions about work and sex. Their Study 1 stopped 59 American students at Yale and 259 British students at Oxford in public areas, primed deliberation, intuition or neither with a scrambled-sentence task, and asked how much respect a virgin and a promiscuous woman deserved. Among Americans the respect gap ran to d = 1.76 after the intuition prime and 1.63 after the neutral prime, and fell to 0.29 after the deliberation prime, F(2, 308) = 6.42, p = .002. British students gave gaps of 0.74, 1.09 and 0.93 with no reliable interaction. Study 2 primed 108 American and 207 Canadian adults in parks in New York State and Ontario with salvation words or neutral words, then had them solve anagrams framed as work. Study 3 reports Asian-American participants rejecting revealing clothing and sexually charged dancing after an implicit work prime, but only where their American identity had been made salient first.

replication.headline: Nothing published under this name has been replicated because nothing has been published under it, and the implicit Puritanism studies nearest to it split: two effects came back at a pooled d of 0.03 and 0.01, and the three that held turned up outside America as well.
replication.detail:
Tierney, Uhlmann and colleagues ran a pre-registered multi-site replication of implicit Puritanism covering more than eight thousand participants in half a dozen nations. Study 1 used 4,098 people recruited by PureProfile in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, oversampling the New England states, plus 2,036 Indian and American workers on Mechanical Turk.

Three effects held. Moral praise for a lottery winner who keeps working rather than retiring came to a meta-analysed d of 0.6524, above the 0.3233 forecast by 221 scientists polled in advance. False memories linking work morality to sex morality came to 0.5053, and were present in the United States, F(1, 1031.8) = 103.8, d = 0.632, and in India, F(1, 997.03) = 10.02, d = 0.201. The preference for the worker over the retiree was stronger under an intuitive than a deliberative framing in the United States, d = 0.543, the United Kingdom, d = 0.175, and Australia, d = 0.329, but not in India, d = -0.067, p = .293.

Two failed everywhere. The moderating role of the lottery winner's age came to 0.032 against a forecast of 0.2461. Salvation priming moved anagram performance in no country, F(1, 1120.58) = 0.034, p = .854, in an online sample of 514 American, 312 British and 298 Australian participants, and it moved nothing in paper-and-pencil laboratory samples at four American colleges, Regina in Canada and Limerick in Ireland. The authors identify both as likely false positives. Protestant faith, religiosity, education and New England residence moderated none of the effects consistently, and where a moderator did reach significance its direction was more often opposite to the theory than consistent with it. Their conclusion is that the results severely undermine implicit Puritanism, because every targeted effect either failed outright or replicated in cultures where it had been predicted not to appear.

A., DeMarree, K., Igou, E. R., Chapman, H., Gantman, A., Vanaman, M., Wylie, J., Storbeck, J., Andreychik, M. R., McPhetres, J., & Uhlmann, E. L. (2021). replicated.weighting: salvation prime effect on work performance, random-effects meta-analysis across the replication samples

limits:
Calling the pattern a bias asserts that the judgement is wrong, and the researchers who measured the judgement decline to say so. Fitouchi and Nettle put the question directly and answer that the current evidence is inconclusive. They note food, sexual and alcohol addiction as a possible kernel of truth, and low self-control's links to crime and to poorer cooperation in experimental tasks, against meta-analytic evidence that self-control does not improve with repeated practice.

Fitouchi and Nettle's samples are American throughout, their mediation analyses are correlational, and the mediation in Study 1 was not pre-specified in the pre-registration. They say their design cannot speak to the origins of puritanical judgement in more puritanical societies. Their figures here are read from the authors' updated preprint on OSF, dated 6 February 2025; the version of record in Cognition is paywalled and was not obtained, so the numbers may have moved.

Tierney and colleagues sampled five countries. They note that their Indian Mechanical Turk sample was 86.4% university-educated, which may have flattened the cultural comparison, and that they cannot rule out the materials being psychologically non-equivalent between the Western and Indian populations.

Searches for the term itself covered Crossref bibliographic queries, PubMed, PubMed Central and web search. The Loewenstein commentary that Wikipedia's definition rests on returned HTTP 403 at SAGE and is listed as closed access by Unpaywall, so nothing is attributed to it here beyond the citation Wikipedia gives it. Wikipedia's own account of what causes puritanical bias offers allostatic load, individualism and cognitive load, all three cited to work on the fundamental attribution error rather than on anything by this name, and its claim that puritanical bias is a subtype of that error has carried a citation-needed tag since May 2025.
misreadings:
The two definitions are not the same claim, and a reader who meets one will be given evidence for the other. Attributing a person's poverty to laziness is an attribution error about causes. Judging masturbation wrong is a moral verdict about an act. Wikipedia's article defines the term the first way and then argues its case with Uhlmann and colleagues' work on Puritan-Protestant intuitions about work and sex, which is about the second.

Wikipedia draws from that work the conclusion that puritanical bias may be an overwhelmingly American phenomenon. The large replication of those studies found the opposite. Praise for needless work and the false-memory link between work and sex morality appeared in India, Australia and the United Kingdom as well as the United States, and the American-distinctiveness claim is the part of implicit Puritanism the replication rejects most firmly.

Fitouchi, Andre and Baumard do not describe puritanical morality as a bias. Their target article argues that condemning harmless pleasures is an output of ordinary cooperation-tracking cognition, on the view that indulgence is read as eroding the self-control that honouring obligations requires. That is a functional account, and it competes with the disgust-based purity accounts it was written against. Weinstein and Baldwin, commenting in the same journal, accept that social evaluations of self-control matter in moral judgement and argue that attributing the whole range of puritanical concerns to self-control is unwarranted.

It is also not the just-world hypothesis, which has its own entry here. That claim is about the observer's need to see suffering as deserved, and it has been tested by having people watch an innocent person suffer. The puritanical claim, in its attribution form, is about the explanations people reach for, and in its moral form it applies to conduct nobody is harmed by.
